readerTitle: Why a subscription business stops growing even when sign-ups never slow
caseNote: 가상 사례 (대형 식료품 체인 안의 밀키트 구독팀, 프로젝트 관리 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 신규 고객 수가 일정해도 고객 기반은 '이탈 수 = 신규 수'가 되는 지점에서 멈춘다. 그 상한선은 신규 ÷ 이탈률로 미리 계산할 수 있고, 이탈을 줄이는 일은 상한선 자체를 옮긴다.
misconception: 매달 신규 고객이 꾸준히 들어오면 고객 수도 계속 같은 속도로 늘어난다. 성장이 멈추면 마케팅을 더 하면 된다.

sources.text: 재고-흐름(stock and flow) 정상상태 계산: 정상상태 고객 수 = 기간당 신규 고객 ÷ 기간당 이탈률. 구독 지표 분석에서 쓰는 표준 계산

factChecks.note: 이 모델은 매달 이탈률이 일정하고 이탈은 월초 고객에게만 적용된다고 단순화했습니다. 실제로는 가입 초기에 이탈이 높고 오래된 고객은 낮은 경우가 많다는 점을 Watch out 카드에 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why a subscription business stops growing even when sign-ups never slow
body: A team adds 200 new subscribers every single month. Same ads, same effort, same result.
After two years, they have fewer than 2,000. Nobody made a mistake in marketing. The answer is in one small number they barely watched.

image.label: A bucket being filled while water leaks from a hole
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 위에서 수도꼭지가 일정하게 물을 붓고, 양동이 옆구리 구멍에서 물이 새어 나감. 양동이 수위는 중간에서 멈춰 있음. 수도꼭지에 "+200 a month", 구멍에 "−10% a month" 라벨. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Will the meal-kit team hit its target?
body: You run the meal-kit subscription team inside a large grocery chain. You sign up 200 new subscribers a month, and each month about 10% of current subscribers cancel.
Head office wants 4,000 subscribers. If nothing changes, what happens?

options.feedback: That counts the people coming in and ignores the people leaving. It's the most common way growth plans go wrong.

options.text: You level off near 2,000 and never reach 4,000
options.feedback: Right. Once you have 2,000 subscribers, 10% leaving is 200 a month, exactly as many as join. Growth stops there.

options.text: You get there, just more slowly than planned
options.feedback: Good instinct that cancellations slow you down. But they don't just slow growth. They put a hard limit on it.

cards.title: Watch the growth fade.
body: Each month, 200 join and 10% of the existing base leaves. The bigger the base gets, the more people leave, until leaving catches up with joining.

cards.title: The retention ceiling
body: Any business with returning customers has a **ceiling**: the size where customers lost each month equal customers gained.
You can calculate it in one line: **new customers per month ÷ share who leave per month**. Here, 200 ÷ 10% = 2,000.
The share who leave is called *churn*. Churn doesn't just slow you down. It decides where you stop.

image.label: A growth curve flattening under a dotted ceiling line
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프. 가로축 "Months", 세로축 "Subscribers". 곡선이 빠르게 오르다가 점선 "Ceiling = 200 ÷ 10% = 2,000" 아래에서 평평해짐. 점선 위 "Target 4,000"은 회색으로 멀리 표시.

cards.title: Two levers, same ceiling, very different cost.
body: To reach 4,000, you could double sign-ups to 400 a month. Or you could halve cancellations to 5%. On paper, both move the ceiling to the same place.
cards.callout: Doubling sign-ups usually means doubling ad spend every month, forever. Fixing why people cancel is often paid for once.

cards.title: Every business with regulars has a ceiling.
body: A gym, an accounting firm with yearly clients, a bakery with morning regulars. Each gains some customers and quietly loses some.

The ceiling explains a familiar feeling: *we work as hard as ever, but we've stopped growing.* Often marketing hasn't weakened. The base has simply grown big enough that normal losses cancel out normal gains.
So when growth flattens, check the leak before you turn up the tap.

cards.title: The ceiling is a rough guide, not a forecast.
body: The math assumes a steady flow of new customers and a fixed churn rate. Real life is messier. New customers often cancel more in their first months, while long-time customers rarely leave.
Your market can also run dry, so sign-ups may fall as you grow. And cutting churn isn't free. Heavy discounts to keep people can cost more than they save.
Use the ceiling to test whether a target is even possible, then look at real customer groups.

cards.title: Now it's a software app.
body: Your project-management app has 10,000 paying teams. You add 500 new teams a month, and 4% of teams cancel each month. That's a net gain of 100 a month.
A colleague says: "At this pace we hit 20,000 in about eight years." What do you say?

options.text: Agreed. 10,000 more at 100 a month is about eight years
options.feedback: The net gain shrinks as you grow, because 4% of a bigger base is more teams. The 100 a month won't last.

options.text: We'll level off near 12,500 unless churn or sign-ups change
options.feedback: Right: 500 ÷ 4% = 12,500. To reach 20,000, you'd need churn near 2.5% or about 800 sign-ups a month.

options.text: Sooner. A bigger base brings more word of mouth
options.feedback: Referrals can raise sign-ups, which does lift the ceiling. But without a number behind it, it's hope, not a plan.

cards.title: Your churn rate decides where you stop.
body: New customers per month divided by the share who leave each month tells you the size your business is heading toward, whatever the plan says.
**Try it today:** estimate how many new customers you gain in a month and what share of your customers you lose. Divide. Is your target above or below that number?
